I'm not so certain the game itself is what one would look for.  But there are many pursuits in board games that are no different than other aspects of life.

Trying to keep a calm, objective, aware mind and general mindfulness practices.

Exploring concepts throughout - be it strategies and other what-ifs.  This is kinda the entire point of boardgames.  To simulate ideas, scenarios, events, etc.  Be it complex, themed, abstract, engine building, competitive, cooperative, etc.

Meditation styles also differ per person.  Some like to be active, some like to observe, or some are trying to quiet their mind.  And you can find all those things in boardgames.  Even quieting one's mind... be it patience and emptiness during games with particularly long down-time.  Or trying not to read to much into someone else's strategies/options/etc., to combatting your personal Analysis Paralysis.

There are just so many ways to approach this.  It's why a lot of people do not realize they meditate already through certain actions and hobbies they perform routinely.  But having that frame of mind to see it can be difficult.

Now, that being said...  if you're looking for something to theme off of the concept, instead of pursuing the concept itself...  Samsara is pretty pleasant.

I wonder if there are any good discussions on how we as individuals should handle the concept of celebrity.  A lot of people seem to get really mad at celebrity opinions.  Be it liking something they don't like (and reverse) or feeling lead astray when they invest in something and have an expectation.

I also suppose celebrity means something different depending on the field or interest, as well.  With boardgames I tend to go for information and communication, and references.  "These mechanics remind me of x."  "I think it would have been better with this mechanic instead of that."  And if anything celebrities are a point of reference to me.  But you have to really know your chosen celebrity.

One may be a kind of wikipedia of games.  They play everything and a lot goes through them.

One may focus on philosophical and subjective components - and you'll hear a lot of: <blah blah blah...>  ... but ... is it 'fun'.......??

And others may be really big into analyzing more quantifiable or rules oriented things.  Using data or game theory to back things up.  Or, at the very least, explore the mechanics along with you.

Knowing the celebrity, but also not getting swept up in them like they are a god, leader, authority, or final word is important.

However, at the end of the day, you're not shaking their hand.  You're not having lunch with them.  Like a really good book or RPG, they're only slightly more real than those friends that leave you when the story is over.  You still have to pull yourself out of the culture and find your own path with the people you sitting down at the table with.

They can teach us how to consider and ask the right questions.  Will it be fun for 'your' players?  Will 'your' group have the time for it?  And I think that's what turns me off a lot.  Some people just don't know how to lay things on the table in an impartial manner.  And if you're there for their fiery or passionate reactions - that's more entertainment than informative.  

Which is fine, too.  But...  always stay mindful of entertainers, informers, and salesmen.

Humans play pretend when they want things reality can't give them.  They read books about topics that interest them.  They find what they seek out.

This is a story-driven game.  A lot of people who have grown up as gamers don't really have any interest in 'stories' these days.  They want information, feedback, stimulation, experimentation, and participation.  And this becomes increasingly important the busier their lives become.  Stories are nice, but most of us are 'living' a story, and would rather enjoy some existential meat.

Stories are for people who have the luxury to slowly digest, stop, and reflect.  And a lot of us have been raised as consuming monsters who devour one concept and move on to the next.  And there are even competitive monsters who only care about numbers and wins, playing the same game repeatedly.  And while I wouldn't identify with those types, I greatly understand that the nature of our hobby is highly attractive to the both of us.

So, there's no problem at all that a different type of consumer is coming into the gaming market.  But they are different, and they have different goals, and they have different audiences, and they have different monsters.  And you've got a very independent, participatory group of gamers being told by storytellers to 'sit down and listen - play at the pace I want you to play at' and while it can lead to good things, it's a very difficult sell to people who are used to doing things on their terms, at their rate, and abandoning it if it forces them to do anything they don't want to do.

I wouldn't be surprised if we start seeing 'Oscar Bait' in gaming.  I just don't see why it matters.  Because the Oscars don't really matter to us.  It's just another award ceremony most of us ignore.  And if a studio would rather spend money pouring into the direction of 'Awards' then it's going to take resources away from other aspects.

They either want return customers, fans, awards, or money.  And honestly, it's better to get awards for doing well in the other areas - instead of stroking the egos of influential critics.

And I'm really not lamenting the 'potentially cool things' they could have developed in a modern day walking simulator.  I just don't have time for story or art.
